title: The peaceful life (Kern ch. 13)
hook: four ways to teach calmly; the jewel in the king's topknot
tomorrow: From the cracks of the earth (Kern ch. 14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, bodhisattvas vowed to keep teaching through insults and threats, and two women were seen and named. Your line: in hard times. What small piece did you keep doing? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-eight.

What's the calmest possible way to say the thing you think matters most? Yesterday's chapter ended with a vow to teach through insults and sticks and swords. A fair question follows: teach how? Shouting back? Winning arguments? In chapter thirteen, Manjushri asks the Buddha exactly that. In the hard age to come, how should a bodhisattva teach this sutra? The Buddha's answer isn't a strategy for winning. It's a way of living, so steady that the teaching can be heard through it. Kern's English calls the chapter the peaceful life. And at the end, there's a king with one jewel he holds back. Today: the peaceful life.
screen: `TEACH HOW?` → `MANJUSHRI ASKS.` → `A KING WITH ONE JEWEL.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Manjushri asks how a bodhisattva can teach the sutra safely, at peace, when times are bad. The Buddha answers with four things to keep. Second, the body and the tongue. Be patient and gentle, he says, not rash, not easily rattled. Don't go chasing after the powerful to win favor. Keep a quiet place to sit and see things as empty, without clinging. And when you speak, don't dwell on the faults of other people, or of other teachers, or of other texts. Don't name people to praise them or tear them down. Answer questions kindly, plainly, in a way that fits the person asking. Third, the mind. No envy, no flattery, no deceit. Don't sneer at people still learning, and don't pick quarrels. Feel compassion for everyone. Look on the Buddhas as fathers and the bodhisattvas as teachers. And keep one wish alive: that people who haven't heard this teaching will someday be brought to it. Fourth, the jewel. A great king wins a war and rewards his soldiers. Fields, villages, towns. Clothes, gold, jewels, elephants, horses. But there's one thing he won't hand out: the jewel in the knot of his hair. If he gave it away lightly, people would be astonished. He keeps it for one soldier whose deed is beyond all the rest. The Buddha says this sutra is that jewel. For a long time he gave other teachings, other rewards. Only now does he take this one out. So the peaceful life is how you carry the jewel: gently, without a fight, without belittling anyone, because what you're carrying is that precious.
screen: `MANJUSHRI ASKS HOW TO TEACH.` · `A CALM BODY, A KIND TONGUE.` · `NO ENVY, NO QUARREL, NO CONTEMPT.` · `THE JEWEL HE KEPT IN HIS HAIR.` · then, large: `THE JEWEL IN THE TOPKNOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: teach one thing calmly. Settle, and let the breath slow. Think of one thing you'll need to explain to someone soon: a chore to a kid, a change to a coworker, a feeling to a partner. Now say it to them in your mind, slowly. Take out any blame. Take out any edge you'd normally add to win. Leave just the thing itself, plain and kind. Say it once more, softer. Then let it go, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The peaceful life. In chapter thirteen, four ways to teach calmly, and a king who keeps one jewel in his hair for the deed beyond all others. Today's word.
Your line: the jewel in the topknot. Today, explain one thing to someone at half your usual speed, with no blame in it. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, this chapter's guidance on teaching gently, without quarreling or speaking ill of others, is studied as a model for how to share the teaching.

fork.setup: you're the king. you've handed out fields, gold and horses. now one soldier stands before you whose deed is beyond all the rest. what do you give?
options: the jewel from the knot of your hair.
nothing more: the rewards are done.
fork.reveal: the king saves the topknot jewel for exactly this. the Buddha says the Lotus is that jewel, kept back and now given.

original.note: Sanskrit: the crest jewel, worn in the knot of hair on the crown.

trapdoor: what you thought: the peaceful life means a quiet retreat away from people.
what it means: four ways to teach in hard times: gentle in body, kind in speech, free of envy, and wishing the teaching for everyone.
what a scholar hears: cudamani, the crest jewel; the king's parable casts the Lotus as the teaching held back until now.
recall: a resting place along the way

notes: Chapter paraphrased from Kern (1884) ch. 13, not quoted (wording unverified). The four peaceful practices are summarized loosely (conduct and sphere, speech, mind, vow); confirm the grouping and that 'don't chase the powerful' fairly renders the instruction not to frequent kings and ministers.

Check the wheel-turning king parable: rewards listed, the crest/topknot jewel withheld because giving it would astonish people, given only to one who has done an extraordinary deed; application to the Lotus.
Original: चूडामणि (cūḍāmaṇi), crest jewel; confirm it is the word in this parable.
Editor: hook said the king 'never gives away' the jewel, which contradicts the parable (he gives it for the one deed beyond all others); now 'holds back'.
